physics_1.title: Physics 1
physics_1.objectives:
The main goal of fundamental courses in physics is to provide tools by which students can learn
how to read scientific material effectively, identify fundamental concepts, reason through scientific
questions, and solve quantitative problems. Physics 1 is the first course of this set. This course
covers the fundamental concepts in Classical Mechanics and Thermodynamics.
physics_1.syllabus:
- Units, Physical Quantities, and Vectors:
The Nature of Physics, Solving Physics Problems, Standards and Units, Unit Consistency and
Conversions, Uncertainty and Significant Figures, Estimates and Orders of Magnitude, Vectors
and Vector Addition, Components of Vectors, Unit Vectors, Products of Vectors
- Motion along a Straight Line:
Displacement, Time, and Average Velocity, Instantaneous Velocity, Average and Instantaneous
Acceleration, Motion with Constant Acceleration, Freely Falling Bodies, Velocity and Position by
Integration
- Motion in Two or Three Dimensions:
Position and Velocity Vectors, The Acceleration Vector, Projectile Motion, Motion in a Circle,
Relative Velocity
- Newton’s Laws of Motion:
Force and Interactions, Newton’s First Law, Newton’s Second Law, Mass and Weight, Newton’s
Third Law, Free-Body Diagrams
- Applying Newton’s Laws:
Using Newton’s First Law: Particles in Equilibrium, Using Newton’s Second Law: Dynamics of
Particles, Frictional Forces, Dynamics of Circular Motion, The Fundamental Forces of Nature
- Work and Kinetic Energy:
Work, Kinetic Energy, and the Work-Energy Theorem, Work and Energy with Varying Forces,
Power
- Potential Energy and Energy Conservation:
Gravitational Potential Energy, Elastic Potential Energy, Conservative and Non-conservative
Forces, Force and Potential Energy, Energy Diagrams
- Momentum, Impulse, and Collisions:
Momentum and Impulse, Conservation of Momentum, Momentum Conservation and Collisions,
Elastic Collisions, Center of Mass, Rocket Propulsion
- Rotation of Rigid Bodies:
Angular Velocity and Acceleration, Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration, Relating Linear
and Angular Kinematics, Energy in Rotational Motion, Parallel-Axis Theorem, Moment-of-Inertia
Calculations
- Dynamics of Rotational Motion:

Torque, Torque and Angular Acceleration for a Rigid-Body, Rigid-Body Rotation About a Moving
Axis, Work and Power in Rotational Motion, Angular Momentum, Conservation of Angular
Momentum, Gyroscopes, and Precession
- Equilibrium and Elasticity:
Conditions for Equilibrium, Center of Gravity, Solving Rigid-Body Equilibrium Problems, Stress,
Strain, Elastic Moduli, Elasticity, and Plasticity
- Fluid Mechanics:
Density, Pressure in a Fluid, Buoyancy, Fluid Flow, Bernoulli’s Equation, Viscosity, and
Turbulence
- Gravitation:
Newton’s Law of Gravitation, Weight, Gravitational Potential Energy, The Motion of Satellites,
Kepler’s Laws and the Motion of Planets, Spherical Mass Distributions, Apparent Weight and the
Earth’s Rotation, Black Holes
- Periodic Motion:
Describing Oscillation, Simple Harmonic Motion, Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion,
Applications of Simple Harmonic Motion, The Simple Pendulum, The Physical Pendulum,
Damped Oscillations, Forced Oscillations, and Resonance
- Temperature and Heat:
Temperature and Thermal Equilibrium, Thermometers and Temperature Scales, Gas
Thermometers and the Kelvin Scale, Thermal Expansion, Quantity of Heat, Calorimetry and Phase
Changes, Mechanisms of Heat Transfer
- Thermal Properties of Matter:
Equations of State, Molecular Properties of Matter, Kinetic-Molecular Model of an Ideal Gas,
Heat Capacities, Molecular Speeds, Phases of Matter
- The First Law of Thermodynamics:
Thermodynamic Systems, Work Done During Volume Changes, Paths Between Thermodynamic
States, Internal Energy and the First Law of Thermodynamics, Kinds of Thermodynamic
Processes, Internal Energy of an Ideal Gas, Heat Capacities of an Ideal Gas, Adiabatic Processes
for an Ideal Gas
- The Second Law of Thermodynamics:
Directions of Thermodynamic Processes, Heat Engines, Internal-Combustion Engines,
Refrigerators, The Second Law of Thermodynamics, The Carnot Cycle, Entropy, Microscopic
Interpretation of Entropy
physics_1.textbooks: 1. Fundamentals of Physics, David Halliday, Jearl Walker, Robert Resnick, 10th edition

calculus_1.title: Calculus 1
calculus_1.objectives:
Calculus 1, consisted principally of one-variable Calculus, Functions, Derivatives, Integrals,
Integration Methods, Complex Numbers, and Infinite Series.
calculus_1.syllabus:
Cartesian coordinates; polar coordinates; complex numbers; addition, product, root & geometrical
representation of complex numbers; polar representation of complex numbers; function; functions
algebra; limit and relevant theorems; infinite limit and limit in infinite; left-hand and right-hand
limit; connectivity; derivative; derivation formula; inverse function and its derivative;
trigonometric functions derivative and their inverse functions; Rolle’s theorem; mean theorem;
Taylor expansion; geometrical and physical applications of derivative; curves and acceleration in
polar coordinates; application of derivative in approximation of equations roots; definition of
integral of continuous functions and piecewise continuous; basic theorems of differential &
integral arithmetic; primitive function; approximate methods of integral estimate; application of
integral in computation of area, length of curve, moment, center of gravity and labor ….(in
Cartesian and polar coordinates); logarithm and exponential function and their derivative;
hyperbolic functions; integration methods such as change of variable, component and
decomposition of fractions; transform of special variables of sequence and numerical series and
relevant theorems; power series and Taylor theorem with remainder.
calculus_1.textbooks:
1. Tom M. Apostol, “Calculus, Vol. 1: One-Variable Calculus, with an Introduction to Linear
Algebra”, John Wiley, 2012.
2. George B. Thomas Jr., Maurice D. Weir, Joel Hass, "Thomas' Calculus (12th Edition)", 2009

differential_equations.title: Differential Equations
differential_equations.objectives:
In this course, the first and second levels of linear differential equations and some nonlinear
differential equations will be introduced, in addition, students will learn about some numerical and
analytical ways to solve Mathematical Problems.
differential_equations.syllabus:
- Introduction
Some Basic Mathematical Models, Direction Fields, Solutions of Some Differential Equations,
Classification of Differential Equations, Historical Remarks
- First Order Differential Equations
Linear Equations with Variable Coefficients, Separable Equations, Modeling with First Order
Equations, Differences between Linear and Nonlinear Equations, Autonomous Equations and
Population Dynamics, Exact Equations and Integrating Factors, The Existence and Uniqueness
Theorem, First Order Difference Equations
- Second Order Linear Equations
Homogeneous Equations with Constant Coefficients, Fundamental Solutions of Linear
Homogeneous Equations, Linear Independence and the Wronskian, Complex Roots of the
Characteristic Equation, Repeated Roots, Reduction of Order, Nonhomogeneous Equations,
Method of Undetermined Coefficients, Variation of Parameters.
- Higher Order Linear Equations
General Theory of nth Order Linear Equations, Homogeneous Equations with Constant
Coefficients, The Method of Undetermined Coefficients, The Method of Variation of Parameters
- Series Solutions of Second-Order Linear Equations
Review of Power Series, Series Solutions near an Ordinary Point, Regular Singular Points, Euler
Equations, Series Solutions near a Regular Singular Point, Bessel’s Equation
- The Laplace Transform
Definition of the Laplace Transform, Solution of Initial Value Problems, Step Functions,
Differential Equations with Discontinuous Forcing Functions, Impulse Functions, and The
Convolution Integral
- Systems of First-Order Linear Equations
Introduction, Review of Matrices, Systems of Linear Algebraic Equations; Linear Independence,
Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, Basic Theory of Systems of First Order Linear Equations
Homogeneous Linear Systems with Constant Coefficients, Complex Eigenvalues, Fundamental
Matrices, Repeated Eigenvalues,
differential_equations.textbooks:
1. E. Kreyszig, Advanced Engineering Mathematics, 1999

2. P. Blanchard, R.L. Devaney, and Co. Hall, Differential Equations, 1st Edition, Brooks/ColePub,
1998

physics_2.title: Physics 2
physics_2.objectives:
The main goal of fundamental courses in physics is to provide tools by which students can learn
how to read scientific material effectively, identify fundamental concepts, reason through scientific
questions, and solve quantitative problems. Physics 2 is the second course of this set. This course
covers the fundamental concepts of Electromagnetism.
physics_2.syllabus:
- Electric Charge and Electric Field:
Electric Charge, Conductors, Insulators, and Induced Charges, Coulomb’s Law, Electric Field and
Electric Forces, Electric-Field Calculations, Electric Field Lines, Electric Dipoles
- Gauss’s Law:
Charge and Electric Flux, Calculating Electric Flux, Gauss’s Law, Applications of Gauss’s Law,
Charges on Conductors
- Electric Potential:
Electric Potential Energy, Electric Potential, Calculating Electric Potential, Equipotential
Surfaces, Potential Gradient
- Capacitance and Dielectrics:
Capacitors and Capacitance, Capacitors in Series and Parallel, Energy Storage in Capacitors and
Electric-Field Energy, Dielectrics, Molecular Model of Induced Charge, Gauss’s Law in
Dielectrics
- Current, Resistance, and Electromotive Force:
Current, Resistivity, Resistance, Electromotive Force and Circuits, Energy, and Power in Electric
Circuits, Theory of Metallic Conduction
- Direct-Current Circuits:
Resistors in Series and Parallel, Kirchhoff’s Rules, Electrical Measuring Instruments, R-C
Circuits, Power Distribution Systems
- Magnetic Field and Magnetic Forces:
Magnetism, Magnetic Field, Magnetic Field Lines, and Magnetic Flux, Motion of Charged
Particles in a Magnetic Field, Applications of Motion of Charged Particles, Magnetic Force on a
Current-Carrying Conductor, Force and Torque on a Current Loop, The Direct-Current Motor, The
Hall Effect
- Sources of Magnetic Field:
Magnetic Field of a Moving Charge, Magnetic Field of a Current Element, Magnetic Field of a
Straight Current-Carrying Conductor, Force Between Parallel Conductors, Magnetic Field of a
Circular Current Loop, Ampere’s Law, Applications of Ampere’s Law, Magnetic Materials
- Electromagnetic Induction:

Induction Experiments, Faraday’s Law, Lenz’s Law, Motional Electromotive Force, Induced
Electric Fields, Eddy Currents, Displacement Current and Maxwell’s Equations,
Superconductivity
- Inductance:
Mutual Inductance, Self-Inductance, Inductors, Magnetic-Field Energy, The R-L Circuit, The LC Circuit, The L-R-C Series Circuit
- Alternating Current:
Phasors and Alternating Currents, Resistance and Reactance, The L-R-C Series Circuit, Power in
Alternating-Current Circuits, Resonance in Alternating-Current Circuits, Transformers
- Electromagnetic Waves:
Maxwell’s Equations and Electromagnetic Waves, Plane Electromagnetic Waves and the Speed
of Light, Sinusoidal Electromagnetic Waves, Energy and Momentum in Electromagnetic Waves,
Standing Electromagnetic Waves
physics_2.textbooks: 1. D. Holliday, R. Resnick and J. Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, 6th edition, John Wiley, 2000

calculus_2.title: Calculus 2
calculus_2.objectives:
The main scope of this course is to teach the students some topics in introductory linear algebra
including matrix algebra and linear transformations and multivariable calculus including
multivariable functions, directional and partial derivatives, velocity and acceleration, tangent plane
and normal gradient line, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, vector field and line integrals,
surface integral, Green's theorem, Divergence theorem, and Stoke's theorem.
calculus_2.syllabus:
Parametric equations; space coordinates; vector and space; numerical product; matrix 3x3 of threeindeterminate linear equations system; operation on lines; matrix reverse; solving equations
system; linear independence; base in R2; R3 linear transform and its matrix; determinant 3x3 and
characteristic value and vector; vector product; second order line and plane equations; two vector
functions and its derivative; speed and acceleration; bending; normal vector to a curve;
multivariable function; directional and partial derivative; tangent plane and normal line to a curve;
multivariable function; directional and partial derivative; tangent plane and projecting line of
gradient; chain of rule for partial derivative; exact differential; second kind and third kind integrals
and their application in geometrical and physical problems; transform of integration arrangement
(without accurate affirmation); cylindrical and spherical coordinates; vector field; curvilinear
integral; surface integral; divergence; curl; Laplacian; potential of green space and divergence and
stochastic.
calculus_2.textbooks:
1. Tom M. Apostol, "Calculus Vol. 2: Multi-Variable Calculus and Linear Algebra with
Applications
to
Differential
Equations
and
Probability",
2012.
2. George B. Thomas and Ross L. Finney, "Calculus and Analytic Geometry (9th Edition)", 1995.

engineering_probability_and_statistics.title: Engineering Probability and Statistics
engineering_probability_and_statistics.objectives:
All branches of engineering need powerful analytic tools to deal with uncertainty, model the
data/information, and predict and analyze underlying systems. Many of the tools necessary for
these analyses have their foundations in probability and statistics. With this in mind, this course
provides elementary probabilistic and statistical concepts and the methods to apply them to
engineering problems.
engineering_probability_and_statistics.syllabus:
- Probability (Axioms, Interpretations, and Properties), Counting Techniques, Conditional
Probability, Independence, Bayes’ Rule
- Discrete Random variables, Probability Mass Function, Probability Distribution Function,
Expectation,
and
Variance
- Especial Discrete Distributions (Uniform, Binomial, Negative Binomial, HyperGeometric,
Poisson)
- Continuous Random Variables, Probability Density Function, Probability Distribution Function,
Expectation,
and
Variance,
Functions
of
a
Random
Variable
- Especial Continuous Distributions (Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, Weibull, Normal)
- Joint Probability Distributions (Discrete and Continuous Cases), Conditional Distributions,
Conditional Expectations, Independence
- Sampling Distributions, Distributions of the Sample Mean, and Sample Variance
- Point Estimation: Maximum Likelihood Method, Method of Moments, Evaluating of Estimators
(Biasedness, Variance, Mean of Squared Errors)
- Interval Estimation: Confidence Intervals for Mean, Variance, and proportion
- Tests of Hypotheses based on a Single Sample (Tests for Mean, Variance, and Proportion, the
Concept of P-Value)
- Tests of Hypotheses Based on Two Samples (Test for a Difference between Two Means, Test
for a Difference between Two Proportions, Test for the ratio of Two Variances, T-Test for Paired
Data)
- Determination of Sample Size in Confidence Intervals and Testing Hypotheses
- Nonparametric Tests (Goodness-of-Fit Test, Test of Independence in Two-Way Contingency
Tables)
- Regression (Simple Linear Regression, Normal Regression Analysis, Correlation)
engineering_probability_and_statistics.textbooks:
1. Walpole and Mayers, Probability and Statistics for Engineering and Scientists, 6th
edition, Prentice Hall. 1998
2. R.V. Hogg and T. Elliot, Probability and Statistical Inference, 4th edition, Mac Millan, 1993

3. Guttman, I., Wilks, S.S., Hunter, J.S. Introductory Engineering Statistics, J. Wiley, 3rd Ed.,
1982.

computer_workshop.title: Computer Workshop
computer_workshop.prerequisites: Introduction to Computing Systems and Programming
computer_workshop.objectives:
Familiarity with accessory systems such as card readers, printers, magnetic tape, discs, and
consoles, manner of work with terminals, familiarity with compilers and editors, familiarity with
JCL language, familiarity with computer organization of a center, familiarity with prepared
software packages such as database, spreadsheet, lotus, familiarity with the important programs of
a system such as a sort, merge, creation and copy of files, etc., familiarity with usage manner of
an operating system of microcomputer

discrete_mathematics.title: Discrete Mathematics
discrete_mathematics.objectives:
Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of a computer system and a discrete mathematics
course seeks to develop proficiency in basic discrete math problem-solving in the way that a
calculus course develops proficiency in basic analysis problem-solving. This course should teach
students to think logically and mathematically, reason and model combinatorially, and use discrete
structures. Some important themes interwoven in this course are mathematical reasoning and
mathematical induction, combinatorial analysis and enumeration, discrete structures, graphs, and
modeling the problems using them.
discrete_mathematics.syllabus:
- Induction and Recursion
Mathematical Reasoning, Mathematical Induction, Strong Induction and Well-Ordering,
Recursive Definitions and Structural Induction, Recursive Algorithms
- Logics and Proofs
Propositional Logic, Propositional Equivalences, Predicates and Quantifiers, Nested Quantifiers,
Rules of Inference, Introduction to Proofs, Proof Methods, and Strategy
- Counting
The Basics of Counting, The Product Rule, The Sum Rule, the Tree Diagram, The Pigeonhole
Principle, Permutations and Combinations, Binomial Coefficients, Binomial Theorem, Pascal’s
Identities and Triange, Vander monde's Identity, Generalized Permutations and Combinations,
Permutations with Repetitions, Combinations with Repetitions, Distributing Objects into Boxes,
Algorithms For Generating Permutations and Combinations
- Advanced Counting Techniques
Recurrence Relations, Modeling with Recurrence Relations, Fibonacci Numbers, The Tower of
Hanoi, Catalan Numbers, Solving Linear Recurrence Relations, Linear Homogeneous Recurrence
Relations with Constant Coefficients, Linear Nonhomogeneous Recurrence Relations with
Constant Coefficients, Divide-and-Conquer Algorithms, and Recurrence Relations, Formal Power
Series, Generating Functions, Counting Problems and Generating Functions, Inclusion-Exclusion,
Applications of Inclusion-Exclusion
- Relations
Relations and Their Properties, n-ary Relations and Their Applications, Representing Relations,
Closures of Relations, Equivalence Relations, Partial Orderings.
- Graphs
Graphs and Graph Models, Incidence and Adjacency Matrices of a Graph, Graph Terminology
and Special Types of Graphs, Complete graphs, Bipartite Graphs, Representing Graphs and Graph
Isomorphism, Connectivity, Euler and Hamilton Paths and Circuits, Algorithm to Construct Euler

Circuits, Ore’s Theorem, Dirac’s Theorem, Shortest-Path Problems, Dijkstra’s Algorithm, Planar
Graphs, Euler’s Formula, Kuratowski’s Theorem, Graph Coloring
- Trees
Introduction to Trees, Rooted Trees, m-ary Trees, Applications of Trees, Huffman Coding, Tree
Traversal, Traversal Algorithms: Preorder, Inorder, Postorder, Spanning Trees, Depth First Search
and Breadth First Search Algorithms, Minimum Spanning Trees, Prim’s Algorithm, Kruskal’s
Algorithm
discrete_mathematics.textbooks:
1. R. P. Grimaldi, Discrete and Combinatorial Mathematics: An Applied Introduction, 5th Edition,
Pearson, 2017.
2. K. H. Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 7th Edition, McGraw-Hill, 2011.
3. S. S. Epp, Discrete Mathematics with Applications, 4th Edition, Brooks Cole, 2010.

data_structures.title: Data Structures
data_structures.objectives:
Familiarity with Information Structures, Effects of Structures in Produced Applications, Selecting
Optimized Inside-Memory Structures, and Organizing Memory based on requirements.
data_structures.syllabus:
Arrays, Vectors, matrices and their application, sparse matrices, heap and stack, queue, lists, linked
lists (linear, cyclic, doubly and multiply linked lists), introduction to trees, binary trees (decisionmaking trees, gaming trees, search trees and …), graphs (representation, sweeping and
applications), Spanning trees, Dynamic memory allocation methods, searching, sorting and
merging algorithms.
data_structures.textbooks:
1. Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein, Introduction to
Algorithms, Third Edition, The MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts 2009
2. A.V. Aho, J.E. Hopcroft, J.D. Ullman, Data Structures and Algorithms, Addison Wesley, 1983

algorithm_design_1.title: Algorithm Design 1
algorithm_design_1.objectives:
The main purpose of this course is to teach the basic concepts and common methods of analysis
and design of algorithms. In this lesson, students learn how to analyze a given problem and find
some possible algorithms to solve it. Then analyze and compare those algorithms in terms of
computational complexity and identify the best ones based on the characteristics of the input
samples. In this lesson, basic algorithms for solving some common problems will be introduced.
algorithm_design_1.syllabus:
Review of essential points of Data Structures, problem-solving methods (for each method some
problems and a special algorithm for the problem shall be represented and analyzed), introduction
to complexity, divide & conquer method (problems to be analyzed: max and min of an array,
multiplication of two n-bit number, Strassen method about matrix multiplication, round robin
algorithm, sorting with Quicksort algorithm), dynamic programming method (matrix
multiplication, traveling salesman problem, polygon triangulation), greedy algorithms(scheduling
problem, Huffman Code, making change), methods based on exhaustive search, alpha-beta
pruning (puzzle, tic-tac-tac), the revelation of methods for problems, graph algorithms(searching
methods of the graph, Dijkstra algorithms, minimum spanning tree, Floyd algorithm, topological
sorting and…), maximum flow networks and other problems.
algorithm_design_1.textbooks:
1. Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein, Introduction to
Algorithms, Third Edition, The MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts 2009.
2. R.E. Neapolitan and K.Naimipour, Foundations of Algorithms using C++ Pseudo Codes, 2nd
Edition,
Johns
and
Bartlett
Publishers,
1998.

introduction_to_computing_systems_and_pr.title: Introduction to Computing Systems and Programming
introduction_to_computing_systems_and_pr.objectives:
Explanation of main computer parts, the concept of software and hardware, algorithms design, and
an introduction to a structured computer programming language.
introduction_to_computing_systems_and_pr.syllabus:
Computer fundamentals, including the role of computers in the modern world and their
applications. Introduction to main computer parts and the concept of software and hardware.
Native data types (Integrals and Floating points). Algorithm design and problem-solving principles
(Flow, selection, and loops). Implanting the algorithm by Pseudo Code. An introduction to a
structured programming language. Constants, variables, computational and logical expressions.
language-specific instructions. Conditional structures. Loops, Arrays, vectors and matrices,
functions, and procedures. I/O and files operations. Implementing simple algorithms by the
programming language. Searching and sorting. Advanced program design.
Programming language: C/C++
introduction_to_computing_systems_and_pr.textbooks:
1. Bjarne Stroustrup, "The C++ Programming Language", Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Stanley B Lippman, "The C++ Primer", Addison Wesley, 2005.
3. Paul Deitel & Harvey Deitel, “C++ How to Program (Early Objects Version)”, Prentice Hall; 9
edition, 2013.

advanced_programming.title: Advanced Programming
advanced_programming.prerequisites: Introduction to Computing Systems and Programming
advanced_programming.objectives:
The purpose of this course is to study the principles and methods (Polymorphism, Inheritance,
Program Samples, and other paradigms of programming) necessary to produce a computer
program with good-quality specifications. In this regard, after covering the top-down design
method to solve the problem, students will be introduced to the concepts and techniques of objectoriented programming as a tool for managing complexity in medium and large-scale applications.
Program performance, testing, and debugging are focused on throughout the course. An objectoriented programming language (such as C++) is used to teach these principles and methods, and
students are introduced to the concepts and techniques of object-oriented programming and
module-based object design, advanced concepts such as graphical user interface design.
advanced_programming.syllabus:
Introduction: Program life cycle, the importance of programming, programming paradigms,
Objected orientation
Object-oriented programming: Description of Objects, Object recognition, Finding implantable
objects in problems, Objects connection, Object-oriented programming language, an Introduction
to C++ and its history
A review of a functional programming language (C++), Polymorphism, inheritance, program
samples
Class and Objects, encapsulation and abstract, C++ classes and their parts (private, public, and
protected), constructor and destructors, derived classes
Polymorphism, polymorphism importance, function polymorphism, operator polymorphism
Inheritance: introduction to inheritance, single and multiple inheritances
Templates: template importance, function templates, derived data type templates
Other programming paradigms: introduction to event-oriented and graphical programming,
windows programming, client-side programming
Program testing and documentation: the importance of testing and documentation, automatic
testing tools, in-line documentation, technical documentation, user manuals
advanced_programming.textbooks:
1. Bjarne Stroustrup, "The C++ Programming Language", Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Stanley B Lippman, "The C++ Primer", Addison Wesley, 2005.
3. Paul Deitel & Harvey Deitel, “C++ How to Program (Early Objects Version)”, Prentice Hall; 9
edition, 2013.

logic_circuits.title: Logic Circuits
logic_circuits.objectives:
This course covers the design and analysis of digital logic circuits including combinatorial and
sequential logic circuits.
logic_circuits.syllabus:
Number systems, binary systems, binary codes, addition, subtraction, multiplication and division,
Boolean algebra, theorems, logic functions, sum-of-products form, product-of-sums form,
Karnaugh maps, logic minimization using K-maps, logic gates (RTL, DTL, TTL) and related
topics (FAN-IN, FAN-OUT), combinatorial circuits design, multiplexers, decoders, comparators,
sequential circuits design, flip-flops, shift registers, counters, synchronous and asynchronous logic
circuits, finite state machines, the timing of sequential circuits
Programming language: Verilog
logic_circuits.textbooks:
1. Morris Mano, Michael Ciletti, Digital Design. 4th ed. Prentice Hall, 2006.
2. Victor Nelson, Troy Nagle, Bill Carroll, David Irwin, Digital Logic Circuit Analysis and Design.
1st ed. Prentice Hall, 1995.

electric_circuits.title: Electric Circuits
electric_circuits.syllabus:
Coulomb's, Ohm's, and Kirchhoff’s laws; electrostatics and electromagnetics; resistance,
capacitance, inductance; series and parallel circuits, independent and dependent voltage and
current sources; energy, power; Superposition, Thevenin, and Norton Theorems; DC and AC;
initial, steady state and transient conditions; frequency selective circuits and resonance; polyphase circuits and transformers.
electric_circuits.textbooks:
1- W. H. Hayt, J. E. Kemmerly, and S. M. Durbin, Engineering Circuit Analysis, 8th Edition,
McGraw Hill, 2011.
2- C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku, Fundamentals of Electrical Circuits, 5th Edition, McGraw
Hill, 2012
3- A. Agarwal, J. H. Lang, Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits, Morgan
Kaufmann Publishers, Elsevier, 2005

logic_circuits_laboratory.title: Logic Circuits Laboratory
logic_circuits_laboratory.objectives:
The logic circuits laboratory is provided with the logic circuits course and its purpose is to acquaint
students with the practical components of logic circuits and how these circuits work and to acquire
skills in the development of circuits and digital systems.
logic_circuits_laboratory.textbooks:
1- C. Roth, L. Kinney, Fundamentals of Logic Design, 7th Edition, Cengage Learning, 2014.
2- F. Vahid, Digital Design with RTL Design, VHDL, and Verilog, 2nd Edition, Wiley, 2011.

engineering_mathematics.title: Engineering Mathematics
engineering_mathematics.objectives:
This course provides mathematical techniques in the more advanced areas of mathematics that are
of most relevance to engineering disciplines.
engineering_mathematics.syllabus:
- Fourier Series, Integrals, and The Fourier Transform
Introduction to Fourier Series, Convergence of Fourier Series and Their Integration and
Differentiation, Fourier Sine and Cosine Series, Other Forms of Fourier Series, Frequency and
Amplitude Spectra of a Function, Double Fourier Series. The Fourier Integral, The Fourier
Transform, Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms, Sturm–Liouville Problems, Eigenfunctions, and
Orthogonality
- Partial Differential Equations
The Method of Characteristics, Wave Propagation and First Order PDEs, Generalizing Solutions,
Conservation Laws and Shocks, The Three Fundamental Types of Linear Second Order PDE,
Classiﬁcation and Reduction to Standard Form of a Second Order Constant Coefﬁcient Partial
Differential Equation, Boundary Conditions and Initial Conditions, Waves and the OneDimensional Wave Equation, The D’Alembert Solution of the Wave Equation and Applications,
Separation of Variables, Some General Results for the Heat and Laplace Equation, An
Introduction to Laplace and Fourier Transform Methods for PDEs
- Complex Analysis
Complex Functions and Mappings, Limits, Derivatives, and Analytic Functions, Harmonic
Functions and Laplace’s Equation, Elementary Functions, Inverse Functions and Branches,
Complex Integrals, Contours, the Cauchy–Goursat Theorem, and Contour Integrals, The Cauchy
Integral Formulas, Some Properties of Analytic Functions, Complex Power Series and Taylor
Series, Uniform Convergence, Laurent Series and the Classiﬁcation of Singularities, Residues and
the Residue Theorem, Evaluation of Real Integrals using Residues, The Inversion Integral for the
Laplace Transform, Conformal Mapping, Conformal Mapping, and Boundary Value Problems
- Calculus of Variations
Maximum or minimum of an Integral, Euler’s equations, Lagrange’s equations, Sturm–Liouville
systems, and Rayleigh-Ritz methods.
engineering_mathematics.textbooks:
1. Michael Greenberg, Advanced Engineering Mathematics, 2nd edition, 1998
2. Erwin Kreyszig, Advanced Engineering Mathematics, tenth edition, 2011

technical_english.title: Technical English
technical_english.objectives:
This subject aims at raising students’ specific language ability in reading and writing academic
texts of their major disciplines. The subject will use reading texts from chapters of books or journal
articles recommended by teachers of different majors for reading comprehension. These texts will
also be used for analysis to enable students to develop an awareness of the genre in that particular
discipline.

computer_architecture.title: Computer Architecture
computer_architecture.objectives:
This course aims to give an understanding of the mechanisms for implementing the programmer's
idealized computer. It builds on the introduction to hardware and simple processors in the Digital
Systems course. The Computer Architecture course aims to describe a broad range of architectural
designs and to contrast them, highlighting the design decisions they incorporate, and how these
design decisions impact program performance.
computer_architecture.textbooks:
1. D A Patterson & J L Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design: The hardware/software
interface, Morgan-Kaufmann (Fifth edition) 2013.

machines_and_language_theory.title: Machines and Language Theory
machines_and_language_theory.objectives:
A presentation of the theory of computing, including coverage of the theory of formal languages
and automata, compatibility, computational complexity, and deterministic parsing of context-free
languages.
machines_and_language_theory.textbooks:
1. Sipser. Introduction to the Theory of Computation. PWS Publishing company, 1997.
2. Linz, An Introduction to Formal Languages and Automata. 3rd edition ed., Jone,s and Bartlett
Publishers, 2001.

operating_system.title: Operating System
operating_system.objectives:
The course provides computer engineering students to understand the ways that applications
interact with the computer hardware as well as different methods of resource management and
their respective algorithms. Further, they will learn of basic mechanisms which are used in the
low-level management of computer systems. Such a student will also learn how to design a system
with the consideration of both hardware and software characteristics and limitations and improve
the quality of programs. The course is a combination of both practice and theory.
Upon successful completion of the course, students will have good insights
1. in different types of computer systems and applications,
2. to design, build, and manage system software,
3. to better discover the reasons for the degraded performance of computer systems and solve the
problem,
4. to propose and implement resource management policies.
operating_system.syllabus:
1) Introduction (Basic terminologies and concepts as well as different computer systems
architectures and software systems, Interrupts, Dual-mode, …)
2) Operating system structures (Different architectures for operating systems, system calls, APIs,
virtualization, and cloud computing)
3) Processes (PCB, context switch, short-term, medium-term, and long-term schedulers, process
creation and communication)
4) Threads (Multithreading models, thread management)
5) Process synchronization (Critical sections and respective solutions, semaphores, monitors,
classic synchronization problems)
6) CPU scheduling (Preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling, CPU scheduling algorithms,
SMP, SMT, multicore scheduling, real-time scheduling)
7) Deadlock handling (Necessary conditions for deadlock, resource-allocation graph, deadlock
prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery)
8) Main memory management (Binding, physical and logical addresses, fragmentation, paging,
TLB, shared pages, segmentation)
9) Virtual memory management (Demand paging, page fault handling, copy-on-write, page
replacement policies, Belady’s anomaly, frame allocation, thrashing, memory-mapped I/O and
files, kernel memory management)
10) Storage management (File system structure, virtual file system, storage allocation methods)
11) I/O management (Interrupts, I/O subsystem, I/O management and performance aspects)
operating_system.textbooks:
1. W. Stallings, Operating Systems, 4th Edition, Prentice Hall, 2001

2. Silberschatz, J.L. Peterson, Operating Systems Concepts, Addison Wesley, 2000 Course

artificial_intelligence.title: Artificial Intelligence
artificial_intelligence.objectives:
AI is an introductory course in Artificial Intelligence. The goal is to acquire knowledge of
intelligent systems and agents, formalization of knowledge, reasoning with and without
uncertainty, machine learning, and applications at a basic level.
artificial_intelligence.syllabus:
Intelligent agents | Problem-solving, complexity metrics | Uninformed search (BFS, DFS, Uniform
cost, depth-limited, iterative deepening) | Informed search (Greedy, A*) | Another search
(simulated annealing, genetic algorithms) | Game playing (minimax, alpha-beta pruning,
nondeterministic games) | Knowledge-based agents | Propositional logic, syntax, semantics,
inference, limitations | First-order logic (including inference, unification, Goedel’s theorem,
generalized modus ponens, resolution, forward chaining, backward chaining, situation calculus) |
Building a knowledge base (ontologies, translation between English and FOL, difficult cases like
events, substances, composite objects) | Logical reasoning systems (Implementing indexing,
retrieval, and unification. Theorem provers. Frame systems and semantic networks) | Planning
(including STRIPS) | Uncertainty | Decision Trees | Fuzzy logic | Neural networks (including
Hopfield, perceptrons, backpropagation)
artificial_intelligence.textbooks: 1. Artificial Intelligence: a modern approach, S. Russell and P. Norvig, Prentice Hall.

operating_systems_laboratory.title: Operating Systems Laboratory
operating_systems_laboratory.objectives:
The goal of this course is to create the right understanding and to learn the techniques of designing
and implementing system programs and operating systems based on an open-source operating
system. Students will get familiar with the implementation of basic design concepts of the
operating system, such as file management, process management, kernel-level programming, and
process synchronization in an open-source operating system, and learn to install and manage an
open-source operating system.
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Compile, install, and manage an open-source operating system
2. Implement the basic concepts of designing operating systems in an open-source operating
system
3. Program in kernel-level
operating_systems_laboratory.syllabus:
1) Introduction: An overview of Linux including its history, versions, Posix, Graphical User
Interface
2) Install and compile a version of Linux: Disk partition, compile, boot load, and use the
application menu and system.
3) Linux file system
4) Standard and advanced Shell
5) Managing Processes and Threads
6) Processor scheduling in Linux
7) Deadlock synchronization
8) Memory management

computer_aided_digital_system.title: Computer Aided Digital System
computer_aided_digital_system.objectives:
Students in the Computer Aided Digital System course will implement and test digital circuits
ranging in complexity from basic logic gates to state machines that perform useful functions like
calculations, counting, timing, and a host of other applications.

signals_and_systems.title: Signals and Systems
signals_and_systems.objectives:
Introduction to the fundamentals of continuous and discrete time signal and system analysis. This
course will cover linear system analysis including impulse response and convolution, Fourier
series, Fourier transforms, sampling, discrete-time signal and system analysis, and Z-transforms.
The student is expected to demonstrate the ability to:
- Apply the convolution theorem for continuous-time signals
- Evaluate the Fourier Series of periodic signals
- Determine the Fourier Transform of energy signals
- Make use of Fourier Transform Properties
- Analyze a discrete-time LTI system using discrete linear convolution
- Use Z-transform for analyzing discrete-time signals and systems
- Convert a continuous-time signal to the discrete-time domain and reconstruct using the
sampling theorem
signals_and_systems.syllabus:
- Introduction
Motivation: Why signal processing is important, Mathematical preliminaries
- Signal Basics
Types of signals, Elementary signals
- Time-Domain Analysis of Continuous-Time Systems
Types of systems, Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, Convolution
- Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS)
CTFS derivation, CTFS properties, Convergence
- Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT)
CTFT derivation, CTFT properties, CTFT, convolution, and LTI systems, Convergence
- Laplace Transform
Region of convergence, Implementing continuous-time systems
- Time-Domain Analysis of Discrete-Time Systems
Types of systems, Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, Convolution
- Time-Domain Analysis of Discrete-Time Systems
Types of systems, Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, Convolution
- Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT)
DTFT derivation, DTFT properties, DTFT, convolution, and LTI systems, Convergence
- Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)
DFT, convolution, and LTI systems, Convergence, Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
- Sampling and Reconstruction
Sampling and the Nyquist theorem, Sinc interpolation, Practical reconstruction

- Z-Transform
Region of convergence, Implementing discrete-time systems
signals_and_systems.textbooks:
1. Alan V. Oppenheim, A. S. Willsky and S. Hamid Nawab, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed.,
Prentice-Hall, 1996.
2. S. Haykin and B. Van Veen, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2003.

compiler_design_and_programming_language.title: Compiler Design and Programming Languages
compiler_design_and_programming_language.objectives:
Designing and building compilers is one of the basic concepts of computer science. Although there
is little variety in the way compilers are made, a wide variety of languages and machines can be
used to make interpreters and translators. In this lesson, the subject of building compilers is
introduced by describing the main components of a compiler, their tasks, and their relationship.
After an introductory introduction to the components of a compiler and the types of grammar, the
various stages of translation, such as lexical, syntactic, and semantic analysis, and code generation
and payment, are described. Students who successfully pass this course will have a good insight
into the following: Familiarity with compiler components and various techniques for their
implementation, understanding of the implementation of programming language commands,
gaining skills in producing optimal programs and fixing programming errors, familiarity and the
use of automated tools in compiler production.
compiler_design_and_programming_language.syllabus:
An introduction to the design and implementation of programming language translators,
Theoretical aspects of language design and translation are discussed, and practically demonstrated
by developing a working compiler.
compiler_design_and_programming_language.textbooks:
1. A. Aho, M. Lam, R. Sethi, and J. Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (2nd
Edition), Prentice Hall, 2006.

computer_networks.title: Computer Networks
computer_networks.objectives:
The purpose of this course is to become familiar with the principles and practice of data
networking; learn how to write applications that use the network; get some understanding of
network internals in a hands-on way; explain the OSI model; recognize the primary network
protocols and distinguish between centralized, client/server, and peer-to-peer systems; and
distinguish between Local Area Networks (LANs) and Wide Area Networks (WANs) and identify
the components used to expand a LAN into a WAN.
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1. To master the terminology and concepts of the OSI reference model and the TCP‐IP reference
model.
computer_networks.syllabus:
Review of fundamental concepts in networking and the Internet
1. Internet protocols and components in the edge and the core of the network
2. Performance concepts such as queue, delay, loss, and throughput
3. Layered architecture
Application Layer
1. Web and HTTP protocol
2. Electronic Mail and SMTP protocol
3. Internet’s Directory Service and DNS protocol
4. P2P applications and P2P file distribution
5. Video streaming and DASH protocol
6. Content distribution and Cache
7. Socket programming
Transport Layer
1. Multiplexing and demultiplexing
2. UDP protocol
3. Principles of reliable transfer and GBN and SR protocols
4. TCP protocol, round-trip time estimation, and flow control
5. Principles of congestion control
Network Layer: Data Plane
1. Data and control planes
2. Router architecture
3. Addressing, IPv4 and IPv6
4. Network address translation and NAT protocol
5. Generalized forwarding (SDN) and OpenFlow protocol
Network Layer: Control Plane
1. LS and DV routing algorithms

2. Intra-AS routing and OSPF protocol
3. Inter-AS routing and BGP protocol
4. SDN control plane
5. ICMP and SNMP protocols
Data Link Layer and LANs
1. The data link layer services
2. Error-Detection and –Correction techniques
3. Multiple access protocols
4. Local area networks, Ethernet, ARP protocol, and VLAN protocol
5. Link virtualization and MPLS protocol
6. Data center networking
computer_networks.textbooks:
1. Computer Networking: a top-down approach / James F. Kurose, Keith W. Ross.6th ed, 2013. 2.
Computer networks / Andrew S. Tanenbaum, David J. Wetherall. 5th ed, 2011.

electrical_measurement_and_circuit_labor.title: Electrical Measurement and Circuit Laboratory
electrical_measurement_and_circuit_labor.objectives:
In this laboratory, students are familiar with the electronic elements of resistors, capacitors, and
inductors, and the operation of electrical measuring devices such as multimeters and oscilloscopes,
as well as other devices used in electrical and electronic circuits such as power supply and signal
generators, as well as measuring parameters such as current. They learn voltage, frequency,
periodicity, phase difference, and power.

computer_architecture_laboratory.title: Computer Architecture Laboratory
computer_architecture_laboratory.objectives:
The purpose of this laboratory is to acquaint students with the concepts presented in the computer
architecture course such as designing digital circuits, how to analyze and debugging them,
designing logic and arithmetic parts of a processor, designing memory units, input/output, data
path, and control unit in a typical processor, Using hardware description languages such as Verilog
and VHDL to describe their structure, synthesize and finally implement on FPGA boards.
computer_architecture_laboratory.textbooks:
1. S. Brown, Z. Vranesic, Fundamentals of Digital Logic with Verilog Design, McGraw-Hill,
2003.
2. B. Parhami, Computer Arithmetic, Algorithms and Hardware Designs, Oxford University Press,
2000.

information_technology_project_managemen.title: Information Technology Project Management
information_technology_project_managemen.objectives:
This course provides participants with the necessary knowledge, tools, and techniques needed to
manage and control projects. It deals with all the processes necessary to plan, manage, execute,
and control projects.

computer_networks_laboratory.title: Computer Networks Laboratory
computer_networks_laboratory.objectives:
The objective of this lab course is to get practical knowledge of the working principles of various
communication protocols. Analyse structure and formats of TCP/IP layer protocols using network
tools such as Wireshark and network simulators.
computer_networks_laboratory.textbooks:
1. J. F. Kurose, Keith W. Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 7th Edition,
Pearson, 2016

real_time_embedded_systems.title: Real Time Embedded Systems
real_time_embedded_systems.objectives:
This course provides an overview of the unique concepts and techniques needed to design and
implement computer systems having real-time response requirements in an embedded
environment. It contrasts the concepts and techniques of real-time and embedded systems with
those of more traditional computer systems. Topics include Basic concepts of real-time and
embedded systems, hardware features, sensors and actuators, programming languages, real-time
operating systems, synchronization techniques, performance optimization, and current trends in
real-time and embedded systems such as incorporating internet connectivity.
real_time_embedded_systems.textbooks:
1. E. A. Lee, S. A. Seshia, Introduction to Embedded Systems – A Cyber-Physical System
Approach. MIT Press, 2016.
2. P. Marwedel, Embedded System Design (Embedded System Foundation of Cyber-Physical
System), Springer, 2011.
3. R. Love, Linux Kernel Development, 2nd Edition, Novell, 2005.
4. S. Seiwert, Real-Time Embedded System and Components, Thomson Learning Inc, Charles
River Media, 2007.

research_and_technical_presentation.title: Research and Technical Presentation
research_and_technical_presentation.objectives:
In this course, students learn systematic research methods and techniques, and skills in presenting
scientific and technical materials. By choosing a subject, students must go through various stages
of compilation and submit a written presentation for it, and in doing so, use information networks
and computer publishing tools. In this course, students will learn the importance and role of
rhetoric in mass communication and will be able to strengthen their sense of self-confidence by
presenting oral material. Students learn different styles of expression and eloquence and gain the
ability to analyze, critique, and evaluate different types of oral communication. Students must
provide several lecture sessions in the classroom.

systems_analysis_and_design.title: Systems Analysis and Design
systems_analysis_and_design.objectives:
Just as solving a mathematical problem requires first identifying its complexities and dimensions,
designing appropriate strategies to solve the problem, and then proceeding to solve it, such as
building computer systems for a set of people (which in many cases may be more complex
mathematical problems) also need to be analyzed and designed before implementation. In this
course, students are introduced to analysis and design skills such as requirements analysis,
feasibility analysis, modeling, process analysis, architectural design, and UI / UX. In addition to
these skills, this course will include computer systems management and production planning skills
such as production methods, process automation, and project management concepts in such
projects.
systems_analysis_and_design.textbooks:
1. L.D. Bentley, K.C. Dittman, and J.L. Whitten. Systems analysis and design methods.
Irwin/McGraw Hill, 2007.
2. K.S. Rubin. Essential Scrum: A practical guide to the most popular Agile process. AddisonWesley, 2012.
3. M. Fowler, C. Kobryn, and K. Scott. UML distilled: A brief guide to the standard object
modeling language. Addison-Wesley Professional, 2004.

database_design.title: Database Design
database_design.objectives:
This course introduces relational database systems. In this course, the students will learn how to
design and create relational databases and how to use them. They will also learn about the internals
of database management systems: how such systems store data, optimize and execute queries, and
process transactions.
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able
1. to understand the basics of a database system and its architecture
2. to design a database for an application: draw an entity-relationship (ER) diagram from a problem
specification, convert the ER diagram to relations, and normalize the relations
3. to write database queries in SQL
4. to write relational algebra and relational calculus expressions for queries
5. to understand how the relations and indexes are stored in a database system
6. to identify useful indexes for a specific database and workload
7. to understand how the queries are optimized and executed in a DBMS
8. to understand concurrency control and recovery in database systems
database_design.syllabus:
Foundations
1. The relational model
2. Relational Algebra and Relational Calculus
3. SQL: Queries, Constraints, Triggers
4. Schema Refinement and Normal Forms
Storage and Indexing
1. Storing Data: Disks and Files
2. Tree-Structured Indexing
3. Hash-Based Indexing
Query Evaluation
1. External Sorting
2. Evaluating Relational Operators
3. A Typical Relational Query Optimizer
Transaction Management
1. Overview of Transaction Management
database_design.textbooks:
1. R. Ramakrishnan and J. Gehrke, Database Management Systems, McGraw-Hill 3rd Edition,
2003.

internet_engineering.title: Internet Engineering
internet_engineering.objectives:
The goal of this course is to cover the basic techniques in developing Web-based and Internetbased programs. Also, important points in the architectural design of a system on an Internet-scale
are examined. In addition, creating Web services, Web 2 concepts and semantic web, social
networks and cloud computing on the Web will also be the subject of this lesson. Another aspect
of this lesson is the provision of web software’s quality requirements such as performance,
scalability, portability, security, and usability.
Students who complete this lesson will be able to:
1. Develop web-based software
2. Respond to architectural challenges in creating Internet-scale applications
3. Use the web as a platform for the development of applications
4. Apply technology frameworks to meet the quality needs of web applications
internet_engineering.syllabus:
1) An Introduction to Web- HTTP protocol - Web page design
2) Create simple web applications (based on Servlet, PHP, or . NET)
3) 3-tier architectural pattern
4) Connection to Databases - Mapping Objects to Relations
5) Domain logic organization
6) Frameworks and layout patterns on the web
7) Manage Sessions
8) Concurrency control on web systems
9) Distributed web systems
10) Clustering and cloud computing
11) Web application security
12) Create Authenticated Web Sites
13) Performance of Web-based systems
14) Web services
15) Semantic web, social networks
16) User interface design on the web
17) Mobile programming on the web

financial_literacy_and_personal_finance.title: Financial Literacy and Personal Finance
financial_literacy_and_personal_finance.objectives:
Financial Literacy and Personal Finance course gives students the knowledge and skills needed to
make informed financial decisions, develop sound financial habits, and manage money effectively.
This course can help students finance their education, purchase a home, or cover medical expenses.
In other words, it can help them reach their goals and maintain financial stability regardless of
life’s ups and downs.

software_engineering.title: Software Engineering
software_engineering.objectives:
The purpose of this course is to study the techniques needed to produce valuable, high-quality
high-productivity software. In this lesson, first, the differences between a product that is produced
by the engineering method and a product that is produced by the artistic methods are expressed.
Then the expectations that an engineering product has to meet are described. Afterward, we will
have an overview of scientific achievements in this field at all stages of software products with an
emphasis on engineering methods of production, including modeling, measurability, evaluability,
validation, and verification. Given the fact that in previous courses students have been less familiar
with the formal descriptions of requirements, measurements, estimates, and tests, this course
focuses more on these subjects. In the end, support activities such as project management,
scheduling, risk management, configuration management, and quality assurance, with emphasis
on their impact on software products, are reviewed. Students who successfully pass this lesson will
have a good insight into
the following:
1. Applying engineering methods to create a quality product
2. Follow the well-known processes of software engineering
3. Application of Software Architectural Design Methods
4. Software Testing at Different Levels
software_engineering.syllabus:
1. An Introduction to Software Engineering
2. Software Development Processes and Models – Iterative Development
3. An overview of software analysis
4. Software design: design principles, patterns, refactoring
5. Software Architecture: Design, Documentation, and Evaluation
6. Software testing
7. Software Quality Management
8. Cost and time estimation
9. Project Management - Human Resources Management - Risk Management
10. Life Cycle Management - Change Management – Configuration Management
11. Agile methods
software_engineering.textbooks:
1. Roger S. Pressman and Bruce R. Maxim, Software Engineering: A Practitioner’s Approach. 8th
ed., McGraw-Hill, 2014.

parallel_programming.title: Parallel Programming
parallel_programming.objectives:
This course is about writing effective programs to harness the unprecedented power provided by
modern parallel computers so that the programs attain the highest possible levels of performance
the machines are capable of. The parallel computers we focus on include multi-core processors as
well as clusters and supercomputers made from them. The programming systems and
methodologies we learn will include OpenMP, Pthreads and CUDA. However, the focus of the
course is not so much on the mechanics of these programming systems as on how to use them to
attain and improve high performance. This performance orientation pervades throughout the
course and is enhanced by several case studies, small enough to understand the lecture format yet
complex enough to illustrate performance issues and trade-offs. The course also teaches an
adequate analytical framework for understanding performance, including performance models,
scalability analysis, and iso-efficiency.

operational_research.title: Operational Research
operational_research.objectives:
Operations Research is a discipline that involves the development and application of advanced
analytical methods to aid complex decisions. This course will provide students with the skills to
be able to apply a variety of analytical methods to a diverse set of applications. By achieving these
objectives, students will be equipped with the necessary knowledge and skills to apply operational
research techniques in a wide range of practical situations. They will be prepared to analyze
complex systems, optimize decision-making processes, and contribute to organizational efficiency
and effectiveness in various domains, including business, engineering, healthcare, logistics, and
finance.
operational_research.syllabus:
1. Introduction to Operational Research
2. Constraint Programming
3. Dynamic Programming
4. Unconstraint Non-Linear Programming
5. Integer Programming
6. Linear Programming

computer_networks_security.title: Computer Networks Security
computer_networks_security.objectives:
Computer networks security is a course designed to teach students about the fundamental concepts
and techniques used in securing computer networks. With the increasing reliance on computer
networks in modern society, network security has become a crucial aspect of information
technology. This course provides an overview of the principles, practices, and technologies used
in computer networks security. The course covers a variety of topics, including cryptography,
authentication, access control, firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention, virtual private
networks (VPNs), and secure network design. Students will learn about the types of vulnerabilities
and attacks that can affect computer networks and the ways to prevent and respond to such attacks.
The goals of this course are:
1. Learning the fundamentals of cryptography
2. Learning the security protocols used in computer networks
3. Learning how security protocols are broken and hacked
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Do basic encryption/decryptions
2. Design secure protocols
3. Analyze the security of protocols
4. Use existing standards to secure the computer networks
computer_networks_security.syllabus:
1- Fundamentals of Cryptography
2- Fundamentals of Computer Networks
3- Key Management
4- Authentication
5- Internet Security
- Web
- Firewall
- Email
- IDS
- VPN / IPSec
- DNS Security
6- Wireless Security
7- Access Control
8- Malware and Attacks
computer_networks_security.textbooks:
1. “Network Security Essentials: Applications and Standards”, William Stallings, 6th ed., Pearson,
2017

knowledge_of_the_environment.title: Knowledge of the Environment
knowledge_of_the_environment.objectives:
Knowledge of the Environment is a course designed to provide students with an understanding of
the principles and practices of environmental science. This course is critical for students who wish
to pursue careers in environmental science, natural resource management, or sustainability.
Throughout the course, students will learn about the fundamental concepts of environmental
science, including ecological principles, biogeochemical cycles, and biodiversity. Students will
gain an understanding of environmental problems and the tools and techniques used to analyze
and solve environmental problems. The course will cover topics such as sustainable development,
climate change, pollution, conservation, and environmental policy.

database_laboratory.title: Database Laboratory
database_laboratory.objectives:
The course aims to cover the fundamentals of databases as seen from the perspective of application
writers. The course covers schema design techniques, SQL, data warehouses, and some aspects of
the NoSQL movement. Also, students will explain the client/server model, and describe the key
components used to implement internet database environments and perform basic database
administration tasks.

introduction_to_software_testing.title: Introduction to Software Testing
introduction_to_software_testing.objectives:
The purpose of this course is to acquaint students with test methods and especially test data
production methods. Also in this course, the necessary tools for the software test are introduced.
introduction_to_software_testing.syllabus:
Introduction to testing methods, Coverage criteria, Graph-based criteria, Criteria based on logic,
Criteria are based on the separation of the input space, Syntax-based criteria, Practical
considerations of software testing, Test tools and software setup for testing.
introduction_to_software_testing.textbooks:
1. P. Ammann, J. Offutt, Introduction to software testing, Cambridge University Press, 2016.
2. P. C. Jorgensen, Software Testing: A Craftsman's Approach, 2nd Edition, CRC Press, 2002.

project.title: Project
project.objectives:
Students choose a professor of the computer engineering department and he/she defines a subject
such as implementing a program on special scientific usage or a subject in computer engineering
to research that, and students must provide an essay and submit their project result and present it.

industrial_training.title: Industrial Training
industrial_training.objectives:
Students must practically get involved in industry and market by working totally specific hours in
an appropriate and defined company in either governmental or private sectors as an intern.

islamic_revolution_in_iran.title: Islamic Revolution in Iran
islamic_revolution_in_iran.objectives:
Theoretical acquaintance with the causes and factors of the Islamic Revolution and analytical study
of cultural, social, and political developments of the Islamic Revolution and subsequent issues.

islamic_thoughts_1_beginning_and_resurre.title: Islamic Thoughts 1 (Beginning and Resurrection)
islamic_thoughts_1_beginning_and_resurre.objectives:
Explain the necessity of Muslim students to pay attention to religion and religious categories,
deepen and expand information and strengthen students' theism and faith in the field of theology
and resurrection.

analytical_history_of_beginning_islam.title: Analytical History of Beginning Islam
analytical_history_of_beginning_islam.objectives:
Familiarity of students with how Islam emerged and spread and the way of transition from an
ignorant society to an Islamic society.

thematic_interpretation_of_the_quran.title: Thematic Interpretation of the Quran
thematic_interpretation_of_the_quran.objectives: Familiarity with some life-giving concepts of the Holy Quran in the form of a thematic attitude.

persian_language.title: Persian Language
persian_language.objectives:
Familiarity with the Persian language and reading literary texts, poetry, and prose in Iranian
Persian literature.

physical_education.title: Physical Education
physical_education.objectives:
Physical Education classes are designed to practice and develop skills in activities that will help
you maintain fitness throughout your life. During the year, you will set and monitor personal
fitness goals that will aid in the development of a personal fitness plan.

english_language.title: English Language
english_language.objectives:
General Language courses, offered at all levels of the Intensive Language Program, seek to
improve students' Language skills in a great variety of discourse settings. Language skills
addressed include listening, fluency development, oral intelligibility, reading, grammar, writing,
and vocabulary development.

family_schematization_and_population.title: Family Schematization and Population
family_schematization_and_population.objectives:
Familiarity of students with the basics of family knowledge and how to form, consolidate, and
excel it as demographic characteristics and their role in improving the quality of life.

islamic_thought_2_prophethood_and_imamat.title: Islamic Thought 2 (Prophethood and Imamat)
islamic_thought_2_prophethood_and_imamat.objectives:
Becoming familiar with instructions in Islam, continuing "Islamic Thought I" discussions.
Expanding students' knowledge about religion, prophethood, Islam, Imamat, and leadership,
which is divided into three sections.

islamic_ethics_principles_and_concepts.title: Islamic Ethics (Principles and Concepts)
islamic_ethics_principles_and_concepts.objectives:
Familiarity of students with the principles and concepts of Islamic ethics in the field of moral
virtues and vices, to acquire virtues and avoid moral vices.

sport_1.title: Sport 1
sport_1.objectives:
This course is designed for the prospective coach, physical education, and/or recreation
professional.

numerical_computation.title: Numerical Computation
numerical_computation.objectives:
This course is an introduction to numerical methods for solving mathematical problems that
arise in Science and Engineering. The goal is to provide a basic understanding of the
derivation, analysis and use of these numerical methods.
numerical_computation.syllabus:
Error Analysis
Some definitions for error, different sources of error, floating point arithmetic, error
propagation
Numerical solution of Nonlinear Equations

digital_signal_processing.title: Digital Signal Processing (DSP)
digital_signal_processing.objectives:
Signal processing is concerned with the representation, transformation, and manipulation of
signals and the information they contain. This course provides an overview of sampling and
discrete-time signals in one or more dimensions; linear shift-invariant systems; the Ztransform; the discrete-time Fourier transform; the discrete Fourier transform and
computationally efficient implementations (fast Fourier transforms); general orthogonal
representations; discrete-time filters: finite and infinite impulse response filters; fixed-point
implementations and finite word-length effects; multidimensional filters and
multidimensional signal processing. After this course, the students should be able to
understand how to analyze a given signal or system using tools such as Fourier transform and
z-transform; what kind of characteristics should we analyze to know the property of a signal
or system; how to process signals to make them more useful; and how to design a signal
processor (digital filter) for a given problem.
digital_signal_processing.syllabus:
Introduction to discrete linear systems
Discrete time signals, Special sequences, Shift invariance, Stability and causality, Impulse
response, Difference equations.
Discrete-Time Fourier Transform and Linear Time Invariant Systems
Transform definitions, Theorems, Frequency response of linear time invariant systems, Phase
and group delays, Matlab computations.
The Z transform
Z-transforms by summation of left, right, and two-sided sequences, Regions of convergence
and Z-transform properties, Inverse Z-transform.
Properties of digital filters
Averaging filter, Recursive smoother, First-order notch filter, Second-order unity gain
resonator.
All-pass filters, Comb filters, Equalization filters, Group delay, linear phase, all-pass,
minimum phase
Fourier transforms, sampling – Part I
Fourier transform review, Sampling continuous-time signals: the sampling theorem, Aliasing,
Re-sampling digital signals.
Fourier transforms, sampling – Part II
A/D conversion and quantization, D/A conversion, Polyphase decomposition, Polyphase DFT
filterbanks, Bandpass sampling
The discrete Fourier transform
Definition of DFT and relation to Z-transform, Properties of the DFT, Linear and periodic
convolution using the DFT, Zero padding, spectral leakage, resolution and windowing in the
DFT.
The fast Fourier transform
Decimation in time FFT, Decimation in frequency FFT.
Digital filter design
Finite impulse response (FIR) filters , Infinite impulse response (IIR) filters
Structures and properties of FIR and IIR filters
IIR - Direct, parallel and cascaded realizations, FIR – Direct and cascaded realizations,
Coefficient quantization effects in digital filters

the wireless channel and the concept of cellular communications are presented. Techniques
formulti-user communication in cellular networks, i.e., Time Division Multiple Access,
Frequency Division Multiple Access and Code Division Multiple Access are investigated. This
course complements Digital Communications.

foundation_of_computer_vision.title: Foundation of Computer Vision
foundation_of_computer_vision.objectives:
Introduction to image processing principles, tools, techniques, and algorithms. Includes topics in
image representation, analysis, filtering, and segmentation, and pattern recognition. Use of image
processing software tools for lab assignments and projects.

blind_source_separation.title: Blind Source Separation (Special Topics in Communication Engineering)
blind_source_separation.objectives:
Course Type: Theoretical Pre-requisites: -
Introduce the framework of well-known Blind Source Separation (BSS) problems and
apply them to various scenarios in fields like telecommunication systems, biomedical
engineering, and control.
Familiarize students with the main scenarios mentioned and appropriate methods for
solving problems within these scenarios.
By the end of the course, students will be familiar with real-world applications of BSS
in fields like telecommunication and biomedical engineering. They will model
problems as mixtures of sources and answer posed questions.
Students will study BSS models in telecommunications, focusing on radio and audio
signals.
Students will study BSS models in biomedical data, including images and brain
signals.
Students will extract suitable features from data, categorize the data, and apply them
in machine learning approaches.

neural_networks.title: Neural Networks
neural_networks.objectives:
Course Type: Theoretical Pre-requisites: -
To familiarize students with the concepts of neural networks, their learning
algorithms, and their applications in classification and regression tasks, as well as
specific and general neural networks.
To provide the necessary skills to use and implement neural networks in major
applications.
Students will become familiar with the basic concepts of neural networks.
The various classes of neural networks with an emphasis on their application in
classification and regression tasks will be introduced.
Concepts such as multi-layer perceptron (MLP), convolutional neural networks
(CNNs), and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) will be introduced.
Students will be familiarized with the basics of training algorithms and regularization
methods.
The advantages and disadvantages of different neural network models will be
discussed, and students will be introduced to various training algorithms.
Students will learn to implement neural networks in real-world scenarios, focusing on
their applications in classification, regression, and pattern generation.

basics_of_machine_learning.title: Basics of Machine Learning
basics_of_machine_learning.objectives: Understanding fundamental concepts of machine learning and pattern recognition, including probabilistic modeling, statistical decision theory, parameter estimation, supervised and unsupervised learning. Developing the ability to formulate classification and regression problems, select and optimize learning models, and apply neural networks, feature selection, dimensionality reduction, and clustering methods.
basics_of_machine_learning.syllabus: Introduction to machine learning concepts and fundamentals of data; Bayesian decision theory, Bayesian classifiers, risk minimization and decision boundaries; Naive Bayes classification; maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation; optimization methods; linear, logistic and nonlinear regression; decision trees; support vector machines (SVM); introduction to neural networks and their applications; introduction to deep vision; principal component analysis (PCA), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and feature selection; clustering and unsupervised learning.

2. Richard O. Duda, Peter E. Hart, and David G. Stork, Pattern Classification, Wiley, 2001.

4. Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction, Second Edition.

foundations_of_data_science.title: Foundations of Data Science
foundations_of_data_science.objectives: Introduction to the data science lifecycle and the principles of collecting, processing, analyzing, visualizing, and modeling data. Developing an understanding of statistical inference, exploratory data analysis, predictive and unsupervised learning, model evaluation, and responsible data-driven decision-making. Familiarity with modern data systems, machine learning operations, neural networks, large language models, and interpretable AI.
foundations_of_data_science.syllabus: Data science lifecycle; sampling, sampling bias, observational and experimental studies, confounding variables; statistical charts; probability theory, conditional probability, Bayes theorem, random variables, expectation and variance, normal and binomial distributions, Monte Carlo simulation; central limit theorem, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and statistical power; data visualization design principles, preattentive attributes, dashboards and storytelling; data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis and feature engineering; SQL, NoSQL, graph databases and MongoDB; big data systems including Hadoop, Spark, Kafka, HBase and Cassandra; modeling principles, prediction versus explanation, training and evaluation splits; linear regression, loss functions and gradient descent; logistic regression; decision trees, random forests, boosting, support vector machines and k-nearest neighbors; regression, classification and clustering evaluation; MLOps, Docker, Kubernetes, MLflow, data and model drift, retraining; unsupervised learning, dimensionality reduction and k-means clustering; feedforward neural networks, convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks; image classification and time series; natural language processing, embeddings, transformers and large language models; retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents; model interpretability and explainability; privacy and ethics in data science.
